_doc: Single source for SD-98's technology choices (compact cut: no drill interlude; the booklet keeps the probes in `drill`). Read by video/src/stack.py for the 5.1 technology slides, the stack table, the fix-slide 'Rejected' lines and the C4 technology labels, and by `stack.py sync` for the booklet and OUTLINE.md regions. Slide `how` is two sentences; the rest goes in `detail` (booklet only).

stack.heading: Log store: MCAP chunks on object storage
stack.title: Logs as immutable one-minute chunks, named by their hash
stack.pick: MCAP files on GCS, one-minute chunks
stack.why: Hashed chunks make a manifest a list of hashes; byte-range reads fetch one topic without a copy.
stack.how: Logs are cut into one-minute MCAP chunks with a per-topic index, each named by its SHA-256. Workers read by byte range and verify the hash.
stack.detail: About 1 GB a log-minute (compressed camera, lidar and radar subsets, illustrative). 20 PB today, plus 1 PB a month; cold chunks move to an archive class after 90 days unless a scenario set references them. A release gate reads about 250 TB in four hours, about 17 GB/s, spread over thousands of chunks: object storage serves that in parallel; the scheduler places workers in the region that holds the chunks.
rejected: HDFS or a shared file system
Another 20 PB system to run, and a copy per job.
Frames are blobs: more cost, a second truth, no byte ranges.
drill: A chunk is re-uploaded after a fix to the logger. What happens to old results?

Nothing changes under them: the fixed chunk has a new hash, so it is a new input. Old manifests still name the old hash, so old runs stay reproducible; a new scenario-set version picks up the new chunk.
a new hash is a new input; old manifests unchanged

stack.heading: Artifact cache: a content-addressed store with an index
stack.title: Stage outputs stored by the hash of everything that made them
stack.pick: CAS blobs on GCS + a Bigtable index
stack.why: A key that hashes everything a stage read hits only when recomputing would give the same output.
stack.how: Key = SHA-256(image digest, params, seed, mode, input keys). The blob is written first, then the index row, so a row always finds a whole blob.
stack.detail: About 100 TB of perception outputs for 20 versions of the gate set, plus exploratory outputs evicted by last access after 30 days. Bigtable rows are tiny (≈ 200 bytes); lookups are batched per scenario. 1 % of hits are re-computed by the auditor and compared byte for byte (challenge 6).
rejected: 100 TB does not belong in memory, and silent eviction loses cited results.
A near-equal for build actions; small outputs, eviction not tied to gate sets.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 7 §7.12 (integrity) and part 9 §9.1 (caching patterns)
drill: A stage reads an environment variable that is not in its key. What breaks?

The cache returns an output computed under a different value: a poisoned hit that no key comparison can see. The fix is hermeticity: stages run in a sandbox where only the manifest's inputs exist, so anything a stage can read is in its key.
hermetic sandbox; nothing readable outside the key

stack.heading: Scheduler: Kubernetes with Kueue
stack.title: Kueue on Kubernetes: quotas per team, priority for the gate
stack.pick: Kubernetes + Kueue, a ClusterQueue per team
stack.why: Admission by quota with borrowing, priority and preemption, on the cluster we already run.
stack.how: Gates run in a reserved, top-priority queue; teams share a cohort and borrow idle quota. Exploratory jobs are preemptible at stage boundaries.
stack.detail: GPU pools by type; gang admission for multi-GPU stages. Fair share by team over a rolling day. A gate needs ≈ 1,040 GPUs for four hours if nothing is cached, ≈ 300 with the usual hit rate; the reserved queue holds 400 and borrows the rest.
rejected: The gate waits behind exploration; one team fills the pool.
Strong at fair share; a separate world from our Kubernetes images.
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 15 §15.4 (priority, quota and preemption) and §15.8 (task leasing)

stack.heading: Results store and catalog: ClickHouse and PostgreSQL
stack.title: Metrics in columns; manifests and scenario sets in rows
stack.pick: ClickHouse for metrics; PostgreSQL for manifests
stack.why: Six billion metric rows a month are scanned by column; manifests and verdicts must be transactional.
stack.how: `metric(run, scenario, name, value)` in ClickHouse, ordered by (scenario, name, run). Manifests, sets and verdicts in PostgreSQL, immutable once written.
stack.detail: A gate decision compares 50,000 scenarios × ~1,000 metrics for two runs: 100 M values, a few seconds in a columnar store. Manifests are rows with content hashes; a scenario set is a versioned list of (chunk range, tags).
rejected: Six billion narrow rows a month: every comparison is a slow scan.
Search over text, not paired numbers across 50,000 scenarios.
summary: columns for metrics, rows for manifests
stack.course: building-blocks course, part 14 §14.9 (columnar storage) and part 8 §8.1 (isolation)

1: it removes one source of difference; threads, GPU atomic adds and the wall clock still reorder the computation.
2: a new build invalidates every stage, and a stage whose dependency changed under the same name serves a stale hit.
3: the release gate waits behind exploration, and one team can fill the cluster.
4: after the ego diverges, the log no longer shows what the other road users would have done.
5: A fixed threshold against yesterday's run
noise moves it, the baseline drifts, and nobody can say later why a build passed.
6: a gate that cannot fail looks exactly like a gate that is passing.
